text.p: An afternoon reversal saw copper end last week challenging the psychological $2,600 per tonne mark, while gold ease on data showing U.S inflation remains contained. The CRB Index closed down 0.19 points at 244.45.

METALS - LME metals each went their own way on Friday afternoon, with copper, nickel and zinc putting in strong performances but the others weak or lacklustre ahead of Third Wednesday pricing next week.

Three months copper reversed in the afternoon and re-attacked the psychological $2,600 per tonne mark, before ending the afternoon kerb $10 higher at $2,590. The market started the morning by looking at the downside, hitting a low of $2,572, but ratcheted higher the rest of the day. It hit a high of $2,604 in the second afternoon ring and ran into profit-taking.

In the short-term the market was overbought, with the 14-day RSI at 77 percent. "The technical indicators are screaming overbought. At best, it will manage to move sideways on Monday," one trader said.

The market streaked up to $2,609 on Thursday on a burst of options covering against a backdrop of tightness and supply disruptions. News that energy problems at Russia's Norilsk was cutting output gave the market another fillip, traders said. A strike at Inco in Canada would deprive the market of 9,000 tonnes of supply each month, analyst Larry Kaplan of Flemings Global Mining Group said. Heavy rains and landslides have hit northern Chile, but Codelco said operations at its Salvador copper mine were normal.
Despite all the bullish news, some analysts were wary of reports China may be tempted to sell at these high levels.
LME copper inventories fell by 6,975 tonnes this week, but Rudolf Wolff analyst Martin Squires said the market should keep a close eye on stocks for signs of a possible turnaround in fundamentals.
Nickel also bounced off its lows, bottoming out at $7,140 before the market digested news of the Norilsk difficulties.It ended up $145 at $7,340, off its high of $7,390.

Zinc also showed resilience, as the bulls won a battle in the morning when good two-way business was seen between $1,353 and $1,356. After it broke loose, prices flew up within $1 of the previous $1,375 peak hit on June 5. They ended $15 stronger at $1,374.

Aluminium extended losses after heavy cash selling in the morning rattled the market, a trader said. Three months shed $29 to $1,586. "I would expect people to be sellers on Monday, it's not looking good," he added. Next support is pegged at $1,575, then $1,540.
Lead was down $6 at $629, after failing on a lacklustre attempt to break the 30-day moving average a few dollars higher.

WHEAT - Prospects for a resumption soon in wheat harvesting in the U.S. Great Plains hard red winter wheat region and persistent satisfactory weather for the soft red winter wheat crop pressured CBOT soft red winter wheat futures to a lower close, traders said. CBOT soft red winter wheat futures closed 1/2 to eight cents per bushel lower, with July down 1/2 at $3.52-1/2. Wet weather slowed combining this week and storms overnight led to early concern about damage to a small portion of the crop in southern Kansas. But analysts said the heavy rains could lead to a reduction in wheat quality localized areas of southern Kansas and probably would not affect the yields very much. The market also was pressured by spillover from Thursday's bearish USDA winter wheat production report. USDA Thursday said 1997 U.S. winter wheat production would total 1.604 billion bushels, above an average of analysts' estimate for 1.579 billion.

GOLD - COMEX gold and silver ended lower with the latest U.S. economic data showing inflation remains no threat to investors. COMEX August gold ended off $0.50 at $343.10, up from a session low of $342.80. In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted at $340.80/$341.30 against the London afternoon fix of $341.40 and Thursday's New York finish of $341.30/80. Earlier, an unexpected fall in U.S. May producer prices of 0.3 percent meant investors felt even less need to hold gold as an inflation hedge, analysts said.

OIL - NYMEX crude futures settled higher on Friday, but sharply below the high of the day as the bears won in a struggle to regain some of the ground lost last week. Traders said the market moved mainly for technical reasons, as speculative funds tried to probe resistance and test support, but leaving unresolved the question of which way the market will move next. July crude futures ended up 14 cents on the day at $18.84, but below the $19.17 high of the day and nearer to the $18.71 low. July futures closed last week at $18.79, $2.09 below the previous Friday's close.

SUGAR - CSCE world sugar futures finished lower Friday after setting new contract highs early on, as continued pressure on the nearby switch dragged the overall market lower. Benchmark October ended off 0.02 cent at 11.32 cents a lb after trading from 11.22 to 11.40, a life-of-contract high. Spot July closed down 0.07 at 11.42, with trades posted from 11.32 to 11.51. The July-October switch shrunk to 0.10 cent by the close, from 0.15 on Thursday.
